title: OS security, privilege and isolation
summary: How operating systems separate programs and users: the kernel boundary, reference monitors, MAC, capabilities, privilege separation, seccomp, namespaces, sandboxes, VMs, and the bugs that break them.
outcomes: Explain why the system call is the only door into the kernel and why kernel bugs outrank all others
Contrast DAC and MAC and read SELinux type rules, AppArmor profiles and their denial logs
Grant one Linux capability instead of root and drop privileges correctly in C
Explain OpenSSH privilege separation and Chrome's broker model, and why each contains a compromise
Describe how seccomp, namespaces and cgroups build a container, and why chroot is not a boundary
Compare containers, gVisor and microVMs by what untrusted code can reach in the host kernel
Recognise confused deputies and TOCTOU races, and fix them with the caller's authority
Explain Dirty Pipe, Baron Samedit, runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels and the layer that stops each

lessons.title: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door

blocks.md:
Every protection in this course rests on one fact: an ordinary program cannot touch the disk, the network card or another program's memory by itself. It has to ask the **kernel**, the core of the operating system that owns the hardware and decides every request.

Tiny example: when you run `cat notes.txt`, `cat` does not read the disk. It asks the kernel to open the file, the kernel checks the permission bits you met in linux-for-security, and only then hands back data. If the check passes, `cat` gets a **file descriptor**, a small number that stands for the open file in every later read; if it fails, `cat` gets an error number and nothing else.

The hardware enforces this split. The processor runs in one of two modes: **user mode**, where privileged instructions (talking to devices, changing memory mappings) are forbidden, and **kernel mode**, where everything is allowed. Programs run in user mode; the kernel runs in kernel mode.

On x86 processors the modes are called **privilege levels**, numbered 0 to 3, and Intel's manual draws them as concentric **rings of protection** with the kernel at the centre (level 0). The manual advises systems that use only two levels to use 0 and 3. That is where the phrases "ring 0" (kernel) and "ring 3" (programs) come from.

How does a user program get anything done? Through a **system call** (syscall): a numbered request to the kernel. The C library wrapper, for example `open()`, copies the syscall number and arguments into registers, then executes a special **trap** instruction that switches the processor to kernel mode and jumps to a handler (`intro(2)`).

The program cannot choose where it lands. At boot the kernel registers a **trap table**, the list of entry points the hardware may jump to (OSTEP, *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*, a free textbook by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, chapter 6). So the only way into kernel mode is through doors the kernel built, and at each door the kernel checks who is asking.

The code in this course is C, the language of the kernel and most system tools. The comments say what each line does, so you can follow it without writing C yourself.

blocks.caption: Run on macOS (the course author's Mac). Both requests reach the kernel and both are refused: EACCES for the file (mode 600, owner root) and EPERM for becoming root. Linux behaves the same way with /etc/shadow.

blocks.title: One program, two system calls, two refusals

scenes.caption: door calls open(). The C library puts the syscall number and the path into registers.
The trap instruction switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's registered entry point. The program cannot pick any other address.
The kernel compares the caller's effective UID (501) with the file's owner and mode (root, 600). No permission bit matches.
The kernel returns an error number and drops back to user mode. The wrapper turns it into -1 with errno EACCES.
Same door for setuid(0). Only a privileged process may set arbitrary user IDs, so the kernel answers EPERM.
Simplified: real kernels also check capabilities and security modules here. The point stands: every request crosses one guarded boundary.

blocks.prompt: A program written in assembly skips the C library and executes the trap instruction itself, with the syscall number for open. Does it get around the permission check?
blocks.reveal: No. The library only packages the arguments; the check happens inside the kernel after the trap. That is why every defence in this course lives in the kernel or below it, and why filters like seccomp (lesson 9) sit at the syscall entry where no program can avoid them.

blocks.md:
**Why kernel bugs are the worst bugs.** The kernel is the thing doing all the checking. A bug in a setuid program gives an attacker that program's power; a bug in the kernel can switch off every check for every process at once, including processes in containers, which share the host kernel (lesson 13). You saw this with Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) in linux-for-security: one kernel race let any local user write to read-only files and so become root. Lesson 16 adds its successor, Dirty Pipe.

The defender view starts here: keep the kernel patched and rebooted, and shrink how much of it untrusted code can reach. Most of this course is about the second half.

User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

blocks.question: Why can't a user-mode program simply jump to the kernel function that writes blocks to the disk?
options: Because the C library refuses to call it
Because kernel functions are written in a different language
Because the processor only enters kernel mode through entry points the kernel registered at boot, and privileged instructions fault in user mode
Because disk writes need a password
blocks.explain: The hardware enforces the boundary. A jump to a kernel address from user mode does not raise privilege; only the trap instruction does, and it always lands on the kernel's registered handler, which checks the caller first.

blocks.question: Which bug is usually the most severe for a multi-user Linux server?
options: A crash in a user's text editor
A memory bug in a kernel system call that any process can make
A memory bug in a setuid program that only root can run
A typo in a log message
blocks.explain: A kernel bug reachable from any process can bypass every permission check, for every user and every container on the host. A setuid program that only root can run gives an attacker nothing new.

lessons.title: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access

blocks.md: Picture an office where every door has its own lock and its own rules, set by whoever installed it. Now picture one guard who stands between everyone and everything, holds the single rulebook, and checks every attempt to open any door. The second office is far easier to reason about. That guard is the idea behind the **reference monitor**.

blocks.title: A reference monitor sits on every path from subject to object

scenes.caption: A subject (a process) wants an object (a file). Under the reference monitor model, there is no direct path between them.
Every request goes to the monitor, which looks up the policy for this subject, this object and this kind of access (read, write, execute).
Allowed: the monitor performs or permits the access and can record it. Fail-safe default: anything the policy does not grant is refused.
Always invoked fails if any path skips the monitor, such as a raw disk device or a buggy driver. Then the policy no longer matters.
Tamper proof fails if the subject can rewrite the monitor or its policy, for example through a kernel memory bug. On Linux the kernel plays the monitor, so both failures mean kernel bugs.

blocks.md:
Three years later Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder, both at MIT, published *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems* (1975). Their design principles still frame OS security:

- **Complete mediation**: every access to every object must be checked. They warn to be sceptical of remembering the result of a check for speed.
- **Least privilege**: every program and user should operate with the least set of privileges needed for the job.
- **Fail-safe defaults**: base decisions on permission, not exclusion; the default is no access.
- **Separation of privilege**: where feasible, require two keys rather than one.
- **Economy of mechanism**: keep protection mechanisms small and simple so their mistakes can be found.

**How real systems map to it.** On Linux the kernel is the monitor, the user/kernel boundary from lesson 1 makes it tamper proof, and system calls are the only way in. On Windows the kernel's access check (a process's access token compared against an object's access list, covered in the optional windows-for-security course) plays the same role.

Linux falls short on the third condition: the kernel is millions of lines, far too big to verify. That is why defenders stack smaller checkers in front of it: seccomp filters (lesson 9), a small hypervisor (lesson 13). The authors of Firecracker, Amazon's minimal virtual machine monitor (lesson 13), give the same reason for writing it instead of reusing QEMU, a widely used open source machine emulator, which they put at more than 1.4 million lines.

Complete mediation is also bent on purpose. Linux checks file permissions when a file is opened; later reads through the open file descriptor are not checked again. Changing a file's mode does not revoke descriptors that are already open.

"We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

blocks.question: To save time, a file server remembers "alice may read report.pdf" for an hour after the first check. Alice is removed from the project after five minutes. Which principle does the cache weaken?
options: Separation of privilege
Open design
Complete mediation
Economy of mechanism
blocks.explain: Complete mediation says every access is checked against the current policy, and Saltzer and Schroeder warn specifically about remembered results. For 55 minutes alice keeps access they no longer have.

blocks.question: A driver bug lets any process overwrite kernel memory, including the code that checks permissions. Which reference monitor condition fails first?
options: Tamper proof
Fail-safe defaults
Least privilege
Small enough to verify
blocks.explain: The monitor itself can be altered by a subject. Once that is possible, nothing it decides can be trusted, which is why kernel memory bugs are so severe.

lessons.title: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks

blocks.md:
Ana owns `notes.txt` and runs `chmod 644 notes.txt`. Now every user on the machine can read it, and nobody asked the administrator. That is **discretionary access control** (DAC): the owner of an object decides who may access it.

Saltzer and Schroeder explain the name (a term they credit to Roger Schell): the pattern is "discretionary" because each user may, at their own discretion, decide who can use what they create. Linux permission bits and ACLs are DAC; the capability `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` is literally "bypass DAC" (`capabilities(7)`). Windows DACLs are DAC too: the D stands for discretionary.

**Mandatory access control** (MAC) is a system-wide policy that subjects cannot change or bypass, whoever owns the file. The idea came from military classification: Saltzer and Schroeder describe managers who need compartments that no employee can undo by editing an access list, and nested levels such as top secret, secret and confidential. The Bell-LaPadula model, a formal model named after its authors David Bell and Leonard LaPadula (cited by Saltzer and Schroeder), formalised that as "no read up, no write down".

One MAC system appears in windows-for-security (an optional course): Windows **integrity levels** are a mandatory check that runs before the DACL and forbids writing up, even when the DACL would allow it.

Why bother on a server? Suppose an attacker takes over a web server running as `www-data`. Under DAC alone the process can read every world-readable file on the machine (other users' notes, configuration, source code) and write anything `www-data` owns. A MAC policy can say instead: *the web server may read web content and write its logs, and nothing else*, no matter what the permission bits say.

Linux adds MAC through the **Linux Security Module** (LSM) framework: hooks at the points in the kernel where access decisions are made, which security extensions fill in. The kernel docs note that "module" is a misnomer: they are chosen when the kernel is built (`CONFIG_LSM`) or at boot (`lsm=`), not loaded later. The main users are SELinux and AppArmor (the next two lessons), plus two smaller MAC modules, Smack (Simplified Mandatory Access Control Kernel) and TOMOYO. The DAC check runs first; if it passes, the LSM is asked.

blocks.title: One open() through DAC, then the LSM hook (simplified)

scenes.caption: Ana's editor opens Ana's own file for reading. The kernel runs the checks in order.
DAC: Ana is the owner and the owner triplet grants read.
The LSM policy also allows it, so open() returns a file descriptor.
Now a hijacked web server tries the same file. The others triplet is r--, so DAC says yes.

scenes.output:
open: Permission denied (EACCES)
audit: denied read by web server domain
scenes.caption: The LSM hook asks the MAC policy, which does not let the web server read home directories. Denied and logged, whatever the mode bits say.
Root passes DAC through CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. The MAC check on line 8 still runs: a confined root process is still confined.

blocks.md: The function names in the figure are invented to keep it short; the order (DAC first, then the security module) follows the SELinux Notebook's description of how a system call is processed. MAC can only take permissions away: an LSM cannot grant an access that DAC refused.

MAC limits damage; it does not remove bugs. The SELinux Notebook is blunt: SELinux "will not stop memory leaks or buffer over-runs" and "will not stop kernel vulnerabilities", though it may contain their effects. A policy also cannot stop anything it allows.

blocks.question: Ana runs `chmod 777 /home/ana/notes.txt`. The SELinux policy does not allow the web server's domain to read files in home directories. Can a compromised web server read the file?
options: Yes, because DAC is checked last and wins
No, because the MAC check runs after DAC and refuses
No, because chmod 777 removes read permission
Yes, because 777 lets everyone read
blocks.explain: Both checks must say yes. DAC passes (others have r), then the LSM hook asks the mandatory policy, which the file's owner cannot override, and it refuses.

blocks.question: Which of these is mandatory, not discretionary?
options: A Windows integrity level that stops a medium-integrity process writing a high-integrity object
A POSIX ACL entry that grants bob read access
A Linux file's permission bits set by its owner
A Windows DACL edited by the folder's owner
blocks.explain: Integrity levels are set by the system and checked before the DACL; the object's owner cannot use them to grant write-up. The other three are all set at the owner's discretion.

lessons.title: SELinux: labels, types and the policy that decides

blocks.md:
**SELinux** (Security-Enhanced Linux) is the main MAC system on Red Hat, Fedora and their relatives. It grew out of FLASK (Flux Advanced Security Kernel), built by the Flux team at the University of Utah with the US Department of Defense, was developed further by the NSA (US National Security Agency) and released as open source.

The core idea is simple: **everything gets a label**, and a central policy says which labels may do what to which other labels. Everything not allowed is denied.

A label is a **security context** with the form `user:role:type[:range]`, for example `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`. For everyday work only the third field matters: the **type**. By convention types end in `_t`.

Processes have types too; a process's type is called its **domain**. The web server runs in the domain `httpd_t`. This style of policy is **type enforcement** (TE): rules are written between a source type, a target type and a class of object, such as `file`, `dir` or `tcp_socket`.

Files get their types from file-context rules in the policy. The reference policy maps `/var/www(/.*)?` to `httpd_sys_content_t` and the nginx configuration under `/etc/nginx` to `httpd_config_t`.

blocks.code:
# file context (reference policy, apache.fc): what label files here get
/var/www(/.*)?      gen_context(system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t,s0)

# a type enforcement rule in the shape the SELinux Notebook shows:
#     allow  source_t  target_t : class  { permissions };
allow httpd_t httpd_sys_content_t:file { getattr open read };

# a policy switch (a "boolean"), off by default (reference policy, apache.te)
gen_tunable(httpd_can_network_connect, false)
blocks.caption: Simplified: the real reference policy writes the allow rule through macros. The boolean decides whether httpd_t may make outgoing TCP connections; an admin turns it on with setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on (Linux only).

blocks.title: Type enforcement: the domain decides, not the user

scenes.caption: The web server process runs in the domain httpd_t. Each file carries a type in its label.
Reading /var/www/html/index.html: an allow rule exists from httpd_t to httpd_sys_content_t for file read. Allowed.
Reading /home/ana/notes.txt (type user_home_t): no rule allows it. Denied with EACCES and an AVC record in the audit log, even if the mode is 777.
Even if the attacker gets root inside the web server, the process is still in httpd_t, so /etc/shadow (shadow_t) stays out of reach.
Outgoing connections depend on the boolean httpd_can_network_connect. Off by default, so a webshell (a script an attacker plants on a web server to run commands) cannot simply call home.

blocks.md:
**Defender view: reading a denial.** SELinux writes refusals to the audit log (`/var/log/audit/audit.log` on most systems) as `type=AVC` records. AVC means access vector cache, the kernel's cache of policy decisions. The example below is from the SELinux Notebook. Read it as: the process `ls` in context `scontext` was denied `getattr` on a `file` whose context is `tcontext`.

A record with `permissive=1` (added in Linux 4.17) means the access was logged but allowed, because the system or that domain is in **permissive** mode. **Enforcing** mode blocks; permissive only watches. `getenforce` prints the current mode.

blocks.code:
type=AVC msg=audit(1243332701.744:101): avc: denied { getattr }
    for pid=2714 comm="ls" path="/usr/lib/locale/locale-archive" dev=dm-0
    ino=353593 scontext=system_u:object_r:unlabeled_t:s0
    tcontext=system_u:object_r:locale_t:s0 tclass=file

# Linux only: find recent denials, show labels, fix a label
ausearch -m AVC -ts recent
ls -Z /var/www/html/index.html
restorecon -v /var/www/html/index.html
blocks.caption: The AVC record is quoted from the SELinux Notebook. restorecon (restore context) resets a file's label from the file-context rules, which fixes the most common cause of denials: a file copied or moved in with the wrong label.

blocks.md: Two habits defeat SELinux: switching it to permissive "to make the app work", and feeding every denial to `audit2allow`, a tool that writes allow rules from log lines. The SELinux Notebook warns that new rules "may start opening holes". First ask whether the label is wrong (restorecon) or a boolean exists for the need.

**Case: runc CVE-2019-5736 and the label that mattered.** This container escape (lesson 16) was announced by Aleksa Sarai, a maintainer of runc, the low-level program that starts containers for Docker and others (containers are explained in lesson 10). The advisory says it was not blocked by the default SELinux policy for Fedora's `moby-engine` package, because container processes there ran as `container_runtime_t`. Fedora's `docker` package and Podman (another container engine) were protected, because they ran container processes as `container_t`. Same kernel, same policy language: the domain a process lands in decides what MAC can do for you.

blocks.question: After a migration the site returns 403 and the audit log shows `avc: denied { read } ... scontext=...httpd_t... tcontext=...user_home_t... tclass=file` for files in /var/www/html. What is the best first fix?
options: Run audit2allow on the log and load every rule it prints
Relabel the files with restorecon so they get httpd_sys_content_t
chmod 777 the web root
setenforce 0, permanently
blocks.explain: The files kept the label of where they were created (a home directory). The policy is right; the labels are wrong. restorecon applies the file-context rule for /var/www, and httpd_t can read them again without widening the policy.

blocks.question: What does a type=AVC record with permissive=1 tell you?
options: SELinux is disabled
The access was blocked and the process was killed
The policy has an explicit allow rule for it
The access would have been denied by policy but was allowed because SELinux is not enforcing for that domain
blocks.explain: In permissive mode SELinux logs what it would deny but lets it happen. It is useful while writing policy and provides no protection.

lessons.title: AppArmor: path-based profiles that confine one program

blocks.md:
**AppArmor** (Application Armor) is the MAC system in Ubuntu's list of security features, and the one Docker, a popular tool for running containers (lesson 10), uses to confine containers by default. Its manual page states its model in one line: it binds access control attributes to **programs** rather than to users. Each confined program has a **profile**, a list of what that program may do; programs without a profile run unconfined, with ordinary DAC only.

The big difference from SELinux: AppArmor rules name **file paths**, not labels. SELinux asks "what type is this file?"; AppArmor asks "what path did the program use?". Paths make profiles easy to read and write, which is a large part of AppArmor's appeal.

blocks.code:
# /etc/apparmor.d/bin.ping  (from the AppArmor project's profiles, trimmed)
abi <abi/5.0>,
include <tunables/global>

profile ping /{usr/,}bin/{,iputils-}ping {
  include <abstractions/base>
  include <abstractions/nameservice>

  capability net_raw,
  capability setuid,
  network inet raw,
  network inet6 raw,

  @{exec_path} mixr,
  /etc/modules.conf r,
  @{PROC}/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/disable_ipv6 r,
}
blocks.caption: A real profile. ping may use two capabilities (lesson 6), open raw IPv4 and IPv6 sockets, map and read its own binary, and read two files. File modes: r read, w write, m map as executable, ix run a program inside the same profile.

blocks.md:
How it is applied (`apparmor(7)`):

- Profiles live in `/etc/apparmor.d/`, named after the program path with `/` turned into `.` (so `/usr/sbin/nscd` becomes `usr.sbin.nscd`), and are loaded into the kernel by `apparmor_parser`.
- A profile attaches when the program is started with `execve`. A process already running unconfined cannot be confined later; restart it.
- Even root is restricted: `apparmor(7)` lists privileged calls a confined process cannot make, such as `init_module`, `ptrace` and `reboot`.

Each profile runs in a **mode** (`apparmor.d(5)`): **enforce** (deny and log `DENIED`), **complain** (allow but log `ALLOWED`, for learning a program's behaviour), or **kill** (deny and also kill the task).

blocks.title: Four requests checked against the ping profile
blocks.code:
profile ping /{usr/,}bin/{,iputils-}ping {
  include <abstractions/base>
  include <abstractions/nameservice>
  capability net_raw,
  capability setuid,
  network inet raw,
  network inet6 raw,
  @{exec_path} mixr,
  /etc/modules.conf r,
  @{PROC}/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/disable_ipv6 r,
}

scenes.caption: ping opens a raw IPv4 socket to send ICMP echo. The network rule matches.
The kernel also needs the net_raw capability for a raw socket. The profile lists it, so the capability check passes this layer too.
Reading a file named in the profile with r is allowed.
A bug in ping is exploited and tries to write /etc/passwd. No rule grants it: in enforce mode the kernel returns EACCES and logs DENIED (log line simplified).
Same request in complain mode: allowed and logged as ALLOWED. Complain mode gives no protection, only a record.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** `aa-status` lists what is loaded and in which mode; the manual page shows this sample. Denials go to the kernel log or the audit log. Docker's documentation shows a real one, raised by the `docker-default` profile that Docker applies to every container unless told otherwise:

blocks.code:
sudo aa-status            # Linux only; sample output from aa-status(8)
apparmor module is loaded.
110 profiles are loaded.
102 profiles are in enforce mode.
8 profiles are in complain mode.
Out of 129 processes running:
13 processes have profiles defined.
8 processes have profiles in enforce mode.
5 processes have profiles in complain mode.

[ 3256.689120] type=1400 audit(1405454041.341:73): apparmor="DENIED"
  operation="ptrace" profile="docker-default" pid=17651 comm="docker"
  requested_mask="receive" denied_mask="receive"
blocks.caption: The DENIED line is quoted from Docker's AppArmor documentation. Watch for profiles stuck in complain mode on production hosts, and for spikes of DENIED lines from one profile: either an update changed the program's behaviour or something is probing.

blocks.md: AppArmor's manual warns that complain mode "does not provide any security, only auditing" and should not be used in a hostile environment, because an attacker's behaviour would be logged and could be added to the profile as if it were normal. Also remember the runc advisory: CVE-2019-5736 was not blocked by the default AppArmor policy. A profile protects only what it was written to cover.

blocks.question: You load a new AppArmor profile for /usr/sbin/mydaemon while mydaemon has been running unconfined for a week. Is the running process now confined?
options: No: profiles attach at execve, so the running unconfined process stays unconfined until it is restarted
Only after the next reboot of the machine
Only if the profile is in complain mode
Yes, immediately
blocks.explain: apparmor(7): a process that is already running unconfined cannot be confined. (Replacing a profile does update processes already running under that profile.) Restart the daemon after loading its first profile.

blocks.question: What is the key design difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
options: AppArmor confines users, SELinux confines programs
AppArmor only works on Windows
AppArmor rules name paths a program uses; SELinux rules name types stored in labels on subjects and objects
SELinux is discretionary and AppArmor is mandatory
blocks.explain: Both are mandatory and both confine programs. AppArmor writes rules in terms of paths, which makes profiles readable; SELinux writes them in terms of types, so a file's label travels with it.

lessons.title: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces

blocks.md:
A web server needs root for exactly one thing: listening on port 80, because ports below 1024 are privileged. Should a bug in its HTTP parser then be able to load kernel modules and read `/etc/shadow`? Traditional UNIX says yes: a process with effective UID 0 **bypasses all kernel permission checks** (`capabilities(7)`).

Since Linux 2.2 the kernel splits root's power into **capabilities**, distinct units that can be enabled one by one. "Capability" here means a named slice of privilege. (Lesson 15 meets an older, different meaning of the word.)

A few you will see constantly, from `capabilities(7)`:

- `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`: bind to ports below 1024.
- `CAP_NET_RAW`: use raw and packet sockets (ping, packet capture).
- `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`: bypass file read, write and execute permission checks. DAC abbreviates discretionary access control, so this is "ignore the permission bits".
- `CAP_CHOWN`: change any file's owner. `CAP_SETUID`: change process UIDs arbitrarily.
- `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`: trace and read the memory of any process.
- `CAP_SYS_MODULE`: load and unload kernel modules, which means running code in ring 0.
- `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`: mount filesystems, set the hostname, create namespaces, many device and filesystem operations, and more.

The man page tells kernel developers not to add to `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` and says it "can plausibly be called 'the new root'". Granting it to a container is close to granting root.

Each thread carries five capability sets:

- **Effective**: what the kernel checks right now.
- **Permitted**: the most the thread may raise into effective. Drop one from permitted and it is gone (unless a later execve grants it again).
- **Inheritable** and **ambient**: what may carry across `execve` to a new program.
- **Bounding**: a ceiling on what any `execve` can ever grant.

Programs can carry **file capabilities** too, stored in the extended attribute `security.capability` and set with `setcap`, so a binary can get one capability instead of being setuid root.

blocks.caption: How execve computes the new permitted set (capabilities(7)). P is the thread before, F the file, & is set intersection and | is union. If the file's effective bit is set, the new effective set equals the new permitted set.

blocks.md: **Worked example.** Ana (no capabilities, full bounding set) runs `/usr/local/bin/webd`, which carries `cap_net_bind_service=ep` (in the permitted set, effective bit on). Inheritable and ambient are empty, so the first and last terms are empty. The middle term is {NET_BIND_SERVICE} intersected with the bounding set, which is {NET_BIND_SERVICE}. The effective bit copies it into effective. Result: webd can bind port 80 and can do nothing else root could.

blocks.code:
# Linux only. An ordinary shell: no capabilities, full bounding set
grep Cap /proc/self/status
CapInh: 0000000000000000
CapPrm: 0000000000000000
CapEff: 0000000000000000
CapBnd: 000001ffffffffff
CapAmb: 0000000000000000

# give one binary one capability instead of making it setuid root
sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=ep /usr/local/bin/webd
getcap /usr/local/bin/webd
/usr/local/bin/webd cap_net_bind_service=ep

# decode the CapEff of a root process in a default Docker container
capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb
0x00000000a80425fb=cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_fowner,cap_fsetid,cap_kill,cap_setgid,cap_setuid,cap_setpcap,cap_net_bind_service,cap_net_raw,cap_sys_chroot,cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap
blocks.caption: Masks computed from linux/capability.h (41 capabilities, CAP_LAST_CAP 40; older kernels show fewer) and Docker's documented default list of 14. Formats follow capsh(1) and cap_to_text(3). setcap and getcap set and show file capabilities; capsh --decode turns a hex mask into names.

blocks.title: Capability bits 0 to 23: root, a Docker container, one service

scenes.caption: A root process on the host: every bit set. Each column is one capability; bit 21 is CAP_SYS_ADMIN, bit 16 CAP_SYS_MODULE.
Root inside a default Docker container: 14 capabilities (11 fall in this range). Mount, module loading and tracing are gone.
webd started from a file with cap_net_bind_service=ep: exactly one bit, number 10.
Someone adds --cap-add SYS_ADMIN to the container to make one mount work. Bit 21 lights up and with it a long list of powers.

blocks.md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

blocks.question: A container needs to bind port 443 as a non-root user. Which change is the least privilege fix?
options: Run it with --privileged
Add CAP_SYS_ADMIN
Run the process as root inside the container
Give the binary (or the process) only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
blocks.explain: Binding below 1024 is exactly what CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE allows. The other options grant far more than the task needs.

blocks.question: Ana's shell has empty permitted, inheritable and ambient sets. Ana runs a binary whose file capabilities are cap_net_raw=p (permitted only, effective bit off). Which capabilities are in the new effective set right after execve?
options: All capabilities, because it is a privileged file
CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_SETUID
None: the file effective bit is off, so the new permitted capability is not raised automatically
CAP_NET_RAW
blocks.explain: P'(permitted) is {NET_RAW}, but P'(effective) equals P'(permitted) only when the file effective bit is set; otherwise it equals P'(ambient), which is empty. A capability-aware program can raise NET_RAW itself later with capset.

lessons.title: Dropping privileges correctly, and sudo's Baron Samedit

blocks.md:
Many daemons need root for a moment at startup: to bind port 22, read a private key or open a log file. After that, the safe move is to become an unprivileged user for good, so that a later bug runs with little power. This is **dropping privileges**, and it is easy to do half-way.

You know real and effective user IDs from linux-for-security. There is a third: the **saved set-user-ID**, a stored copy of the effective UID that lets a process switch its effective UID back later (`credentials(7)`). If a daemon changes only its effective UID, root is still sitting in the saved slot, and injected code can simply switch back.

blocks.caption: The fixed version compiles cleanly (checked on macOS with stub declarations for the Linux-only calls setresuid, setresgid and prctl). Order matters because changing GIDs and groups needs privilege that the UID change removes.

blocks.md:
Why the fixed version works:

- **Groups, then GID, then UID.** `setgroups` and `setresgid` need privilege (`CAP_SETGID`). Once the UIDs are no longer 0, that privilege is gone, so they must come first. rule POS36-C of the SEI CERT C Coding Standard (from Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute) (Observe correct revocation order) says the same.
- **All three IDs.** `setresuid` sets real, effective and saved at once. When all three leave 0, the kernel clears the permitted and effective capability sets too (`capabilities(7)`).
- **Check every return value.** The `setresuid(2)` page calls omitting the check "a grave security error"; CERT POS37-C requires verifying the drop.
- **no_new_privs.** After `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS`, `execve` will never grant privileges again: setuid bits and file capabilities stop working for this process and its children. The flag cannot be unset.

blocks.title: Watching the IDs during a correct drop

scenes.caption: The daemon starts as root, binds its port and opens its files.
Supplementary groups are cleared while the process still has the privilege to do it.
All three group IDs become the service group 999.
All three user IDs leave 0, so the kernel also empties the permitted and effective capability sets.
The self-test asks for root back. It must fail; if it ever succeeds, the program stops instead of running half-dropped.
No setuid program or file capability can raise this process or its children again.

blocks.md:
**Case: Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156).** `sudo` is the opposite of a dropped process: a setuid-root program that must read untrusted input (the caller's arguments) while running as root. On 26 January 2021 the Qualys research team disclosed a heap buffer overflow in it. Any local user could exploit it, with or without a sudoers entry and without knowing a password. The bug was introduced in July 2011 and affected sudo 1.8.2 to 1.8.31p2 and 1.9.0 to 1.9.5p1 in their default configuration (the sudo project lists 1.7.7 to 1.7.10p9 as affected too).

The mechanism: in shell mode (`-s` or `-i`) the sudo front end escapes special characters with backslashes, and the policy plugin removes those escapes again, copying arguments into a heap buffer sized from their lengths. If an argument ends in a single backslash, the copy loop steps over the string's terminating zero byte and keeps copying whatever follows. Normally impossible, because the front end had escaped every backslash; but run as `sudoedit -s`, the shell flag was set while the escaping step was skipped.

blocks.title: Baron Samedit: an unescape loop runs past the end (simplified)

scenes.caption: One argument ends in a lone backslash: A, B, backslash, then the zero byte that ends the string. Other data follows in memory. The buffer was sized for 4 bytes.
A and B are copied one by one.
At the backslash, the next byte is not a space, so the loop skips ahead one byte to the terminator and copies it, then advances again: from now points past the end of the string.
The loop only stops at a zero byte, so it copies X, Y and Z, which were never counted in the buffer size. Bytes land past the end of the heap buffer: an overflow inside a root process.
The fix: never skip onto the terminator, check the remaining space before every write, and unescape only when a command really runs through a shell.

blocks.caption: Trimmed from the Qualys advisory and the fix commit by Todd C. Miller, the sudo maintainer (logging calls shortened). Three independent fixes: the shell-mode condition now matches the escaping condition, the loop cannot step onto the terminator, and every write is bounds-checked.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Patch to sudo 1.9.5p2 or 1.8.32 or a vendor build; the sudo project said there was no workaround. Its advisory gives a safe check: on a vulnerable sudo, `sudoedit -s /` prompts for a password or prints `sudoedit: /: not a regular file`; a patched one prints a usage message. The bigger lesson: sudo parsed hostile input as root, before any policy decision. The next lesson shows the design that avoids that. Ubuntu 25.10 also made sudo-rs, a rewrite of sudo in the memory-safe language Rust, its default sudo.

blocks.question: A daemon calls `seteuid(1000)` after startup and nothing else. An attacker gets code execution in it. What can the attacker do?
options: Nothing more than uid 1000 could
Load kernel modules, but not read files
Only read files owned by 1000
Call seteuid(0) and become root again, because the saved set-user-ID is still 0
blocks.explain: seteuid changes only the effective UID. The saved set-user-ID still holds 0, and an unprivileged process may set its effective UID to its saved one. A real drop changes all three IDs (setresuid) and then checks that setuid(0) fails.

blocks.question: Why must setresgid come before setresuid when dropping from root?
options: It does not matter
setresuid resets the groups automatically
Group IDs are checked first by the kernel
After the UIDs leave 0 the process loses the capability needed to change GIDs, so a later setresgid would fail and leave root's group in place
blocks.explain: Changing GIDs and supplementary groups needs CAP_SETGID. Dropping the UIDs first clears the capabilities, so the group change fails, and if the return value is not checked the process keeps group 0.

blocks.md:
Dropping privileges works when root is needed only at startup. The SSH server needs root throughout a login: to check passwords against `/etc/shadow`, sign with the host's private key and finally become the logged-in user. Yet its most dangerous code, the parser for bytes arriving from anyone on the internet, needs no privilege at all.

**Privilege separation** splits one program into a small privileged part and a larger unprivileged part that talk through a narrow interface. Saltzer and Schroeder's least privilege, applied inside a single program.

blocks.title: OpenSSH today: listener, privileged monitor, unprivileged child

scenes.caption: A client connects. The listener runs as root but only accepts connections and enforces limits; it does not parse SSH protocol data.
For each connection the listener starts sshd-session, the privileged monitor for this connection. It also never parses network bytes itself.
The monitor starts sshd-auth, which chroots to /var/empty and switches to the dedicated sshd user before reading a single network byte.
All SSH protocol parsing happens in sshd-auth. When it needs privilege (does this user exist, is this password right, sign with the host key) it sends a request to the monitor.

If a parser bug is exploited, the attacker holds an unprivileged process in an empty, read-only chroot. It cannot read keys or shadow, and the monitor only answers requests that fit its state machine.
After a successful login the monitor forks a child that drops to the user (uid 1000) and runs the session. The monitor stays as root for jobs such as allocating terminals.

blocks.code:
# pre-authentication, from OpenSSH's README.privsep
  PID    PPID   UID CMD
 1436       1     0 sshd: /usr/sbin/sshd -D [listener] 1 of 10-100 startups
47077    1436     0 sshd-session: djm [priv]
47078   47077   107 sshd-auth: djm [net]

# post-authentication
47077    1436     0 sshd-session: djm [priv]
47091   47077  1000 sshd-session: djm@pts/1
47092   47091  1000 -bash

# preparing the privsep account (README.privsep): no shell, owns nothing
mkdir /var/empty && chown root:sys /var/empty && chmod 755 /var/empty
groupadd sshd
useradd -g sshd -c 'sshd privsep' -d /var/empty -s /bin/false sshd
blocks.caption: Process lists quoted from README.privsep. The [net] process runs as UID 107, the dedicated sshd user. The split into sshd and sshd-session arrived in OpenSSH 9.8 (which also removed the option to disable privilege separation); sshd-auth was split out in 10.0.

blocks.md:
README.privsep lists the goals: reduce the privileged attack surface by handling untrusted data in unprivileged code, make it easy to wrap the exposed component in an OS sandbox (seccomp on Linux, lesson 9), share little between the halves, and contain attacks to the unprivileged process. The privsep user "must not be shared with any other system service, should own no files" and have a shell that refuses logins, and the chroot directory must be empty and not writable by that user. Otherwise a compromised child would have something to read or write.

The same broker pattern reappears in Chrome (lesson 12), and in Firecracker's jailer (lesson 13).

Privilege separation protects only the code that was moved into the unprivileged half. regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387, covered in linux-for-security) was a signal-handler race in sshd's privileged code which, in Qualys's words, "is not sandboxed and runs with full privileges". That is why OpenSSH keeps shrinking the privileged parts: the 9.8 and 10.0 splits move more code out of them.

blocks.question: An attacker exploits a parser bug in sshd-auth before authentication. Which outcome does privilege separation aim for?
options: Read access to /etc/shadow but no write access
A crash of every SSH session on the host
Control of an unprivileged process in an empty chroot that can only send the monitor the requests its state machine accepts
Root shell on the server
blocks.explain: The network-facing child runs as a dedicated unprivileged user inside /var/empty. Anything privileged must go through the monitor, which refuses out-of-order or unexpected requests and decides authentication itself.

blocks.question: Why does README.privsep insist that /var/empty is empty and not writable by the sshd user?
options: Because chroot only works on empty directories
So that a compromised child finds nothing to read and cannot plant files that a privileged process might later trust
So that log files go elsewhere
To save disk space
blocks.explain: The chroot is the child's whole view of the filesystem. Empty means nothing to steal; not writable means nothing to tamper with or leave for others.

lessons.title: seccomp: filtering system calls at the door

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 said the system call is the only door into the kernel. Linux has hundreds of them; Docker's documentation counts "300+". How many does a program really need? The Firecracker paper puts a trivial Linux program at 15 distinct syscalls and a typical Ubuntu installation at 224 (plus 52 `ioctl` calls; `ioctl`, input/output control, is the catch-all call for device-specific requests). Every syscall a process can make is kernel code it can reach, and kernel bugs are the worst kind.

**seccomp** (secure computing) lets a process tell the kernel which doors it will never use again.

It has two modes:

- **Strict mode** (Linux 2.6.23): after entering it, the thread may call only `read`, `write`, `_exit` and `sigreturn`; anything else kills it. Built for number-crunching on untrusted data that arrives through an already-open pipe.
- **Filter mode** (Linux 3.5), often called **seccomp-bpf**: the process installs a small program in **BPF** (Berkeley Packet Filter, a tiny instruction set first used to filter network packets in the kernel). The kernel runs it on every syscall the process makes.

The filter sees a `struct seccomp_data`: the syscall number `nr`, the architecture `arch`, the instruction pointer and the six raw arguments. It returns an action. In precedence order: `KILL_PROCESS`, `KILL_THREAD`, `TRAP` (send SIGSYS), `ERRNO` (fail with a chosen error), `USER_NOTIF`, `TRACE`, `LOG`, `ALLOW`.

blocks.title: A seccomp-bpf filter (from seccomp(2)) deciding three calls

scenes.caption: Instruction [0] loads the architecture. [1] compares it with x86-64: it matches, so execution continues.
[2] loads the syscall number. [3] checks that no x32 bit is set (59 is far below the limit).
[4] matches the blocked number, so [5] returns ERRNO with 99. execve never runs; the program sees error 99. Output quoted from the man page.
Another call: [4] does not match, jumps to [6], ALLOW. The kernel runs write normally.
A call made with the 32-bit calling convention has different numbers. The arch check jumps straight to [7] and kills the process, so nobody slips past by switching ABI.

blocks.md:
That filter is a **deny-list**: it blocks one call and allows the rest. `seccomp(2)` strongly recommends the opposite, an **allow-list**, because a deny-list must be updated every time a dangerous syscall is added, and the same effect can often be reached another way (block `open` and the attacker uses `openat`). Two more rules from the man page and kernel docs:

- Always check `arch`, and on x86-64 handle the x32 numbering bit (x32 is a second ABI, or application binary interface, that runs 64-bit code with 32-bit pointers and marks its syscall numbers with bit 30), or a deny-list can be bypassed.
- A process must first set **no_new_privs** (lesson 7) or hold `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. This stops an unprivileged user from installing a filter and then running a setuid program that misbehaves under it. Filters are inherited by children and can only be added, never removed.

blocks.caption: libseccomp builds the BPF program, arch check included, from readable rules (seccomp_init(3), seccomp_rule_add(3)). Afterwards only read, write to fd 1 and exit work; anything else kills the process, even hidden libc calls (malloc may call brk), so set up first.

blocks.md:
**Containers use this by default.** Docker's default profile is an allow-list: `defaultAction` is `SCMP_ACT_ERRNO`, and a long list of names is set to `SCMP_ACT_ALLOW`. Docker says it disables "around 44 system calls out of 300+", including `mount`, `kexec_load`, the module-loading calls, `keyctl` and `add_key` (the kernel keyring is not namespaced), `unshare` and namespace-creating `clone` flags, and the `io_uring` calls (a fast asynchronous I/O interface), blocked after container escapes. `/proc/<pid>/status` shows `Seccomp: 2` for a process in filter mode.

**Limits.** The kernel documentation states plainly: "System call filtering isn't a sandbox." A filter cannot follow pointers, so it cannot see the path string passed to `openat`; deciding *which files* is the job of an LSM or of Landlock (unprivileged self-sandboxing for file access). A filter also does nothing about bugs in the syscalls it allows.

**Defender view.** Since Linux 4.14 each kill by a filter goes to the audit log (`type=SECCOMP`, with the syscall number); a burst from one service deserves an alert.

blocks.caption: Excerpt of Docker's default seccomp profile (moby/profiles default.json; the first rule lists 359 names in the current file). The second rule shows argument filtering: socket is allowed only for some address families.

blocks.question: A filter blocks `open` by number but allows everything else. The sandboxed program needs to read /etc/shadow. What happens?
options: It cannot read any files
It calls openat (or another route) instead, which the deny-list never mentioned
seccomp follows the path and blocks shadow
The kernel blocks it because shadow is sensitive
blocks.explain: Deny-lists fail open: anything not named is allowed. That is why seccomp(2) recommends allow-lists. And even an allow-list cannot inspect the path, because filters cannot dereference pointers.

blocks.question: Why does the kernel require no_new_privs (or CAP_SYS_ADMIN) before an unprivileged process may install a seccomp filter?
options: To make filters faster
So that a user cannot apply a filter and then run a setuid-root program, making it fail in unexpected, exploitable ways while it holds root
It does not; any process may install filters freely
Because BPF needs root to compile
blocks.explain: With no_new_privs set, execve can no longer raise privileges, so a filter installed by an unprivileged user never constrains a program running with more privilege than that user had.

lessons.title: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers

blocks.md:
A container is not a small virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel shows a private view of the system, limits in what it may consume, and usually restricts with dropped capabilities, a seccomp filter and an LSM profile. The Firecracker paper lists the pieces: cgroups for resource limits, namespaces for views, seccomp-bpf for syscalls, chroot for the filesystem. Underneath, every container on a host shares **one kernel**.

A **namespace** wraps a global resource so that processes inside see their own isolated instance of it; changes are visible inside and invisible outside (`namespaces(7)`).

blocks.title: Eight namespace types, one kernel

scenes.caption: A host process and a container process. Both run on the same kernel; namespaces decide what each one sees.
PID namespace: process IDs. The container's first process is PID 1 inside and some other number outside, and it cannot see or signal host processes.

labels.hv: nginx is PID 4242; all PIDs visible
labels.cv: nginx is PID 1; only its own tree

scenes.caption: Mount namespace: the list of mount points. The container gets its own root filesystem (the image) and its own /proc.
Network namespace: network devices, protocol stacks and ports. Two containers can both listen on port 80.
UTS namespace: hostname and NIS domain name.
User namespace: UID and GID numbers. UID 0 inside can map to an unprivileged UID outside, and capabilities inside apply only to resources that namespace governs.
IPC namespace: System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues, so containers cannot attach to each other's shared memory.
Cgroup namespace: the container sees its own cgroup as the root of the cgroup tree.
Time namespace: per-namespace offsets for the boot-time and monotonic clocks. The calendar clock is not namespaced.

labels.cv: boot clock with its own offset

scenes.caption: What no namespace changes: the kernel itself. Every system call from every container runs in the same kernel, so one kernel bug reaches them all.

blocks.code:
# Linux only. Examples and outputs quoted from unshare(1).

# a new PID namespace (plus a fresh /proc): the command is PID 1
# unshare --fork --pid --mount-proc readlink /proc/self
1

# as an ordinary user, a user namespace where you are root
id -u; id -g
1000
1000
unshare --user --map-root-user \
        sh -c 'whoami; cat /proc/self/uid_map /proc/self/gid_map'
root
         0       1000          1
         0       1000          1
blocks.caption: The uid_map line reads: inside ID 0 maps to outside ID 1000, for a range of 1 ID. Root inside is plain user 1000 to the rest of the system.

blocks.title: A user namespace ID map (from /etc/subuid 1000:100000:65536)

scenes.caption: Inside IDs on top, the host IDs they stand for below. Inside 0 maps to the user's own UID 1000.
Inside 1 to 65535 map to the subordinate range starting at 100000, so inside 65535 is host 165534. None of these is privileged on the host.
A file created by inside UID 1 shows up on the host owned by 100000 (the unshare(1) example shows exactly this). Root inside cannot touch host files owned by real root.

blocks.md:
**Why user namespaces matter for security.** The runc advisory for CVE-2019-5736 (lesson 16) says the escape *is* blocked by correct use of user namespaces where host root is not mapped into the container. The flip side: creating namespaces exposes kernel code to unprivileged users, so Docker's default seccomp profile blocks `unshare` and namespace-creating `clone` flags inside containers, and Ubuntu (from 23.10) restricts them on the host: an unprivileged program gets no capabilities in a new user namespace unless its AppArmor profile allows `userns`.

**cgroups** (control groups) organise processes into a hierarchy whose resource use can be limited and monitored (`cgroups(7)`). Namespaces control what a container can *see*; cgroups control how much it can *use*, which stops one tenant from starving the host. In cgroup version 2, limits are plain files:

blocks.code:
# Linux only, as root, cgroup v2, with the controllers enabled in the
# parent's cgroup.subtree_control
mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo
echo 50M          > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max   # hard limit; OOM killer inside the group
echo 100          > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/pids.max     # fork/clone fail with EAGAIN beyond 100
echo "50000 100000" > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max    # 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period
echo 4242         > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs # move process 4242 in
blocks.caption: From the kernel's cgroup-v2 docs: memory.max defaults to max (at the limit the OOM, out-of-memory, killer ends processes in the group), pids.max makes fork() and clone() return EAGAIN, and cpu.max takes a quota and period (default "max 100000"). A fork bomb in demo stops at 100 processes.

blocks.question: A process is root inside a user namespace (mapped to UID 1000 outside). It tries to set the system's calendar clock. What happens?
options: It changes the clock only for the container
It succeeds, because it has all capabilities in its namespace
It succeeds only inside a time namespace
It fails, because capabilities in a user namespace apply only to resources governed by that namespace, and the system clock is not one
blocks.explain: user_namespaces(7) uses this very example: changing the system time is governed by CAP_SYS_TIME in the initial namespace. Time namespaces offset only the boot and monotonic clocks.

blocks.question: Which statement about containers is accurate?
options: cgroups hide other containers' processes
Each container runs its own kernel
Namespaces give a private view and cgroups limit resources, but all containers on a host share the host kernel
A PID namespace stops kernel bugs from being reachable
blocks.explain: Views come from namespaces, limits from cgroups, and the kernel is shared. That shared kernel is why lesson 13 looks at gVisor and microVMs.

lessons.title: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why

blocks.md:
`chroot` (change root) is the oldest isolation trick on UNIX: it changes the directory that paths starting with `/` resolve from, so a process that chroots into `/srv/jail` sees `/srv/jail/etc` when it opens `/etc`. It needs `CAP_SYS_CHROOT`.

The Linux manual page is unusually direct: chroot "changes an ingredient in the pathname resolution process and does nothing else". It "is not intended to be used for any kind of security purpose, neither to fully sandbox a process nor to restrict filesystem system calls."

The man page lists the holes:

- It does **not** change the current working directory, so `.` can still be outside the new root. With that, root can walk back out of a chroot (the man page shows the three commands).
- It does **not** close open file descriptors, and "such file descriptors may allow access to files outside the chroot tree".
- If a directory is moved out of the chroot while a process sits in it, the process can follow it out.

So chroot helps only when combined with other controls. OpenSSH's sshd-auth chroots to an empty directory **and** drops to an unprivileged user that cannot call chroot again. Containers instead use a mount namespace and `pivot_root`, which swaps the root mount for the whole namespace, plus everything from the previous lessons. Even then, an open file descriptor that points outside is a door.

**Case: Leaky Vessels (CVE-2024-21626).** On 31 January 2024 the runc maintainers (runc, from lesson 4) disclosed a container escape found by Rory McNamara of Snyk, a security company. Snyk named it and three bugs found alongside it in BuildKit (Docker's image builder) "Leaky Vessels".

In runc 1.1.11 and earlier, several file descriptors leaked into `runc init`, the process that becomes the container, including a handle to the host's `/sys/fs/cgroup` (leaked since v1.0.0-rc93). If the container's working directory was set to `/proc/self/fd/7/` (the number varies), the new process started with its working directory **in the host's filesystem**, after `pivot_root` had seemingly put it inside the container. runc also never checked that the final working directory was inside the container.

A malicious image could hide this behind an innocent-looking `WORKDIR` (the image's starting directory) that is really a symlink, a file that points to another path, to `/proc/self/fd/7/`. Variants used `runc exec` or overwrote host binaries. The advisory scores the worst variant 8.6 (high).

blocks.title: Leaky Vessels: one descriptor that should have been closed

scenes.caption: runc init starts on the host side and opens the host's /sys/fs/cgroup. Without O_CLOEXEC, that descriptor survives into the container process.
runc joins the container's namespaces and pivot_roots into the image. Everything the process sees by path is now the container.
The image's WORKDIR is a symlink to /proc/self/fd/7/. chdir follows it through the leaked descriptor.
The container process now has a working directory in the host's mount namespace. Relative paths from there reach the whole host filesystem.
runc 1.1.12: descriptors are opened with O_CLOEXEC, all internal ones are closed before execve, and runc refuses to start if the working directory is outside the container.

blocks.caption: O_CLOEXEC (close on exec) makes a descriptor close automatically at execve. The advisory recommends other runtimes add exactly these two checks: getcwd() not returning ENOENT, and close_range(3, UINT_MAX, CLOSE_RANGE_CLOEXEC) before starting the container process.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Upgrade runc to 1.1.12 or later (Docker shipped fixes in moby 25.0.2 and 24.0.9). The advisory's workarounds: allow only a working directory of `/` (it cannot be a symlink), and run only trusted images. For the `runc exec` variant there is no practical workaround except patching. When reviewing images, a `WORKDIR` or path that is a symlink into `/proc/self/fd` is a red flag.

chroot changes how paths are looked up, nothing more. Open file descriptors, the working directory and root's privileges all ignore it. Real filesystem isolation needs a mount namespace, no privilege to undo it, and no handles that point outside.

blocks.question: Why can't an ordinary, non-root process inside a chroot use the chroot-then-cd-up trick from the man page to escape?
options: Because calling chroot itself requires CAP_SYS_CHROOT, which the process lacks
Because the kernel kills processes that call cd
Because cd .. is disabled in a chroot
It can; chroot never stops anyone
blocks.explain: The escape relies on calling chroot again. That needs CAP_SYS_CHROOT, which is why OpenSSH combines its chroot with a drop to an unprivileged user.

blocks.question: Which of runc 1.1.12's fixes also protects against file descriptor leaks nobody has found yet?
options: Renaming /sys/fs/cgroup
Closing all internal descriptors before execve and checking that the working directory is inside the container
Marking the one known cgroup descriptor O_CLOEXEC
Disabling WORKDIR in Dockerfiles
blocks.explain: Fixing the known leak removes one hole. Closing every non-stdio descriptor and verifying the working directory with getcwd stop the whole class, which is why the advisory recommends them to other runtimes.

lessons.title: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS

blocks.md:
A **sandbox** combines the mechanisms so far to run code you expect to be compromised. Chromium's design document is explicit: for threat modelling, the sandboxed code should be considered malicious once execution gets past a few early calls in `main()`. The browser parses hostile web pages all day; the question is not whether a renderer bug will be exploited but what the attacker gets when it is.

The sandbox's promise, from Chromium's FAQ: a bug in sandboxed code cannot install persistent malware in the user's account or read and steal arbitrary files.

Chromium's design rests on a few principles: do not invent a new OS security model, use the one the OS has; **least privilege**; **assume sandboxed code is malicious**; and "emulation is not security".

It works at process granularity with two roles. The **broker** (always the browser process) holds privilege, sets each target's policy, spawns the targets and performs policy-allowed actions for them. The **targets** (renderers and other sandboxed processes) run the risky code with almost no rights. Anything they need they request over IPC (inter-process communication), and the broker checks it against policy. The design doc notes the interception that forwards calls is for compatibility, not security: security comes from the target's lack of rights.

blocks.title: Broker and target: the renderer asks, the browser decides

scenes.caption: The user saves a download. The renderer cannot open files itself, so it asks the browser process over IPC.
The request fits policy (a user-initiated download into Downloads). The broker, which has the user's rights, opens the file and hands over just that handle.
A malicious page exploits a renderer bug. The attacker's code tries to open an SSH key directly. The renderer's token (Windows) or namespaces and seccomp (Linux) make the kernel refuse.
It asks the broker instead. The broker must validate the request, not trust it: the key is outside policy.
What the sandbox cannot stop: a bug in the kernel itself, reached through a syscall the renderer is still allowed to make. Chromium's FAQ says so directly.

blocks.md:
**On Windows** the target gets a restricted token, a job object, a separate desktop and an integrity level, Windows mechanisms covered in windows-for-security (not a prerequisite here): a token lists a process's identity and rights, a job object caps a group of processes, and the desktop isolates its windows. The most restrictive renderer token has no privileges, every SID (security identifier, the number that names a user or group) except the logon SID is deny-only, and its integrity level is **Untrusted** (`S-1-16-0x0`), below Low. The design doc says it is "near impossible" to find a resource the OS will grant to such a token, so almost everything a renderer uses is opened by the broker and its handle duplicated in.

**On Linux** Chromium layers mechanisms: a setuid helper (`chrome-sandbox`) puts the renderer in new PID and network namespaces, chroots it to an empty read-only directory, marks it undumpable, drops all capabilities and then drops from root to the user; on top of that comes a seccomp-bpf filter, which, Chromium notes, also shrinks the kernel attack surface.

**macOS App Sandbox.** Apps declare **entitlements**, signed key-value pairs that list the resources they need (network client, user-selected files, camera). The App Sandbox is required for the Mac App Store. A sandboxed app gets a private container directory and no general access to the user's home folder; a file the user picks in an Open dialog becomes accessible through the `files.user-selected` entitlements. Apple's documentation says to verify with `codesign`. Here are two built-in apps on the author's Mac:

blocks.code:
% codesign -d --entitlements - /System/Applications/TextEdit.app
Executable=/System/Applications/TextEdit.app/Contents/MacOS/TextEdit
[Dict]
	[Key] com.apple.application-identifier
	[Value]
		[String] com.apple.TextEdit
	...
	[Key] com.apple.security.app-sandbox
	[Value]
		[Bool] true
	[Key] com.apple.security.files.user-selected.executable
	[Value]
		[Bool] true
	[Key] com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write
	[Value]
		[Bool] true
	[Key] com.apple.security.print
	[Value]
		[Bool] true

% codesign -d --entitlements - /System/Applications/Calculator.app | grep -A2 network
	[Key] com.apple.security.network.client
	[Value]
		[Bool] true
blocks.caption: Real output (macOS, trimmed with ...). TextEdit is sandboxed and may read and write only files the user chooses; Calculator may make outgoing network connections.

blocks.md: **iOS and iPadOS** go further, per Apple's Platform Security guide: **all** third-party apps are sandboxed; each app gets a unique, randomly assigned home directory; apps and most system processes run as the unprivileged user `mobile`; the operating system partition is mounted read-only; and entitlements are signed into apps so they "can't be changed". Apple uses entitlements so that system daemons can do specific privileged operations without running as root, which "greatly reduces the potential for privilege escalation". That is capabilities and privilege separation, built into the platform.

A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

blocks.question: A Chromium renderer is fully compromised. Which outcome does the sandbox design aim to prevent?
options: The page displaying wrong content
The attacker running code in the renderer at all
Exploitation of bugs in the OS kernel
The attacker reading arbitrary files or installing persistent malware in the user's account
blocks.explain: The design assumes renderer compromise. The goal is that the compromised process has no rights to files or persistence, and everything it asks the broker is checked. Kernel bugs are explicitly out of scope.

blocks.question: Why does an iOS app's entitlements list need to be signed?
options: To make the app start faster
So that a compromised or modified app cannot grant itself new privileges by editing the list
Because Apple charges per entitlement
Entitlements are not signed
blocks.explain: Entitlements are signed with the app, so changing them breaks the signature. The platform can then trust the list when deciding what the app may do.

lessons.title: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker

blocks.md:
Lesson 10 ended on the weak point of containers: one shared kernel. The other classic answer is the **virtual machine** (VM): each workload gets its own complete kernel, running on virtual hardware. Underneath sits a **hypervisor**, also called a **virtual machine monitor** (VMM; OSTEP notes the two terms mean the same thing), which uses the processor's hardware virtualisation features to keep each guest kernel inside its box. On Linux the in-kernel part is **KVM** (Kernel-based Virtual Machine), and a user-space VMM such as QEMU supplies the virtual devices.

The Firecracker paper, written by Amazon Web Services engineers (Alexandru Agache, Marc Brooker and colleagues), sorts isolation into three families: containers, which share a kernel; virtualisation, where each workload runs in its own VM; and language VMs, where a runtime such as a JavaScript engine does the isolating.

The security difference, in the paper's words: in Linux containers "untrusted code calls the host kernel directly, possibly with the kernel surface area restricted (such as with seccomp-bpf)". In virtualisation, untrusted code gets full access to a **guest** kernel, which is treated as untrusted, and hardware virtualisation and the VMM limit what the guest can reach. A guest kernel bug compromises one guest; the attacker then faces the much smaller VMM interface.

The cost was always weight: a full VM boots slowly and carries a large device model. QEMU, the usual VMM, is "more than 1.4 million" lines of code as of version 4.2, by the paper's count, which is a lot of trusted code.

blocks.title: Three ways to run untrusted code on one host

scenes.caption: Container: the app's system calls go straight to the host kernel, narrowed by seccomp, an LSM, namespaces and capabilities.
gVisor: the app's system calls are caught by the Sentry, an application kernel written in Go that implements the Linux interface itself. The Sentry uses only a small set of host calls.
MicroVM: the app talks to its own guest kernel. The guest reaches the host only through virtual devices in a minimal VMM (Firecracker) and KVM.
A host kernel bug in a syscall the container may still make is directly reachable from the container app. That is the Dirty Pipe scenario of lesson 16.

Defence in depth inside the VMM: the jailer starts the VMM in a chroot, in its own PID and network namespaces and without privileges, and Firecracker then loads a seccomp allow-list on each of its threads.

blocks.md:
**gVisor** (a Google project) keeps the container's process model but moves the system interface into a per-sandbox **application kernel** written in Go, a memory-safe language, running in user space. [Its docs](https://gvisor.dev/docs/) say it is "not a syscall filter" and "not a VM in the everyday sense". The Sentry implements Linux system calls itself and makes few host calls: no new sockets unless host networking is on, and under directfs (default since 2023) only file opens relative to directories that a helper, the Gofer, hands it. It ships as an OCI (Open Container Initiative, the standard container format) runtime, `runsc`, so Docker and Kubernetes can use it. The trade: some compatibility and performance for a much smaller host attack surface.

**Firecracker** keeps KVM but replaces QEMU with a new, minimal VMM built for serverless workloads. The paper reports under 5 MB of memory overhead per microVM, boot to application code in under 125 ms, and up to 150 microVMs created per second per host. It runs AWS Lambda and Fargate, and has been open source since December 2018.

blocks.title: How much kernel interface is really needed? (Firecracker paper)

scenes.caption: Distinct system calls needed by a trivial Linux program, and by a typical Ubuntu 15.04 installation (Tsai et al., cited by the paper). A container exposes everything its filter allows.

In the 2020 paper the VMM's seccomp filter allowed only 24 system calls, each with argument filtering, plus 30 ioctls (22 for the KVM API). Today Firecracker loads per-thread filters itself; the main VMM thread's list has about 58.

blocks.md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

blocks.question: A new host kernel bug is reachable through a syscall that Docker's default seccomp profile allows. Which workload is most directly exposed?
options: A Firecracker microVM, because KVM is in the host kernel
A gVisor sandbox, because the Sentry is written in Go
A normal container, because its system calls go straight to the host kernel
None: namespaces hide the kernel
blocks.explain: A container's syscalls are handled by the host kernel. In gVisor the app's calls are handled by the Sentry, and in a microVM by the guest kernel, so the host bug is not directly reachable from the app.

blocks.question: Why does Firecracker run its own VMM inside a jailer (chroot, namespaces, no privileges) and under a tight seccomp allow-list?
options: Because KVM requires it
Defence in depth: if a guest exploits a VMM bug, the attacker lands in a process with almost no access to the host
Because the guest kernel is trusted
To make boot faster
blocks.explain: The paper describes the jailer as protection against unwanted VMM behaviour, such as a hypothetical bug that lets the guest inject code into the VMM. Every layer assumes the one in front of it can fail.

lessons.title: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs

blocks.md:
Every check so far assumes the kernel is the real one. An attacker who replaces the bootloader, or loads their own kernel module (a **rootkit**, malware that hides itself by modifying the kernel, often lives there), *becomes* the reference monitor, and can hide from everything above it. Two ideas defend the kernel itself: verify everything that runs before and inside it, and stop even root from changing the running kernel.

**UEFI Secure Boot** (UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, the firmware interface of modern PCs) checks each binary loaded at boot against trusted keys stored in firmware. Most x86 machines ship with Microsoft's certificates, and Linux distributions build on that (Ubuntu security documentation).

blocks.title: The Ubuntu secure boot chain, one signature at a time

scenes.caption: Firmware loads shim, a small first-stage loader signed by Microsoft, and checks that signature against the certificates in firmware.
shim carries Canonical's certificate and uses it to check GRUB (GRand Unified Bootloader), the bootloader. A failure at any stage stops the boot.
GRUB loads the kernel, a signed EFI binary, and checks its signature. Note from the docs: initrd images (the initial RAM disk the kernel unpacks at boot) are not validated.
The kernel checks every module before loading it. Ubuntu's own modules carry Canonical's signature; locally built ones need a Machine Owner Key (MOK).
An unsigned module, say a rootkit, is refused. insmod and modprobe fail with an error.

blocks.md:
**Module signing** is a kernel feature in its own right: modules are signed at build time and the kernel checks the signature on load, using X.509 certificates (the standard certificate format, as used in TLS) for the public keys. With `CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE` or the boot option `module.sig_enforce=1`, only validly signed modules load. Without it, unsigned modules still load but **taint** the kernel (marked `E`), a flag that records the kernel is no longer pristine.

**Kernel lockdown** (Linux 5.4, `kernel_lockdown(7)`) goes one step further: it stops even root from reaching the running kernel image. Under lockdown `/dev/mem`, `/dev/kmem` and `/dev/kcore` are closed, kprobes (kernel tracing hooks) and BPF are restricted, only signed modules load, kexec (starting a new kernel from the running one) accepts only signed kernels, and debugfs (a kernel debugging filesystem) is off. It logs lines like `Lockdown: X: Y is restricted, see man kernel_lockdown.7`. This is the line between "root" and "the kernel", the same line lesson 6 drew around `CAP_SYS_MODULE`.

**Runtime knobs.** Many hardening settings are `sysctl` values under `/proc/sys`, documented in the kernel's admin guide:

- `kernel.kptr_restrict`: hide kernel addresses printed via `%pK` (2 hides them from everyone). Kernel exploits usually need to know where kernel code and data sit in memory, so leaked addresses help attackers.
- `kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1`: only `CAP_SYSLOG` may read the kernel log.
- `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled`: 1 disables unprivileged `bpf()` and cannot be undone; 2 disables it but an admin may change it later.
- `kernel.perf_event_paranoid`: limits performance monitoring for users without `CAP_PERFMON`; the default is 2.
- `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1` (Yama is a small LSM that limits ptrace): a process may only `ptrace` its own descendants, so one compromised app cannot read the memory of your SSH agent.
- `fs.protected_symlinks`, `fs.protected_hardlinks`, `fs.protected_regular`: block the classic `/tmp` link races (lesson 15).
- `kernel.modules_disabled = 1`: no more module loading or unloading, ever, until reboot.

blocks.code:
# /etc/sysctl.d/60-hardening.conf   (Linux only; apply with: sudo sysctl --system)
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1
kernel.perf_event_paranoid = 2
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
fs.protected_symlinks = 1
fs.protected_hardlinks = 1
fs.protected_regular = 2
fs.suid_dumpable = 0

# one-way switch: run late in boot, after every needed module is loaded
# sysctl -w kernel.modules_disabled=1
blocks.caption: Values and meanings from the kernel's sysctl documentation (kernel.html, fs.html) and the Yama LSM page. randomize_va_space = 2 also randomises the heap; suid_dumpable = 0 stops processes that changed privilege from dumping core.

blocks.md: Secure boot proves *what* booted, not that it is bug-free. BlackLotus (2023) carried old, validly signed but vulnerable Windows boot managers to switch Secure Boot protections off, because they had not been revoked yet. Keep the firmware's revocation list (DBX) and certificates current (Microsoft's 2011 Secure Boot CAs expire in 2026; the 2023 CAs replace them), and never disable `module.sig_enforce` or lockdown "temporarily".

blocks.question: An attacker has root on a server with kernel lockdown enabled and module signature enforcement on. What stops them loading a rootkit module they compiled?
options: Secure boot scans the disk at runtime
The rootkit must be in /lib/modules
The kernel refuses modules that are not validly signed with a trusted key, even for root
Nothing: root can do anything
blocks.explain: With enforcement, the kernel itself checks the signature at load time. Root controls the filesystem but does not hold the signing key, so the module is refused.

blocks.question: What does `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1` prevent?
options: All use of gdb
Root from debugging anything
A compromised process from attaching to unrelated processes of the same user, such as an SSH agent, to read their memory
Core dumps
blocks.explain: Under classic rules any process can ptrace other dumpable processes of the same UID. Mode 1 limits attachment to descendants (or explicitly declared debuggers), while CAP_SYS_PTRACE still allows admins to attach.

lessons.title: What goes wrong: the confused deputy and TOCTOU races

blocks.md:
Some failures are not missing checks but checks applied to the wrong authority, or at the wrong moment. Two classic patterns explain a large share of local privilege bugs.
