**The confused deputy.** Norm Hardy, an architect at Key Logic who earlier worked at Tymshare, a commercial timesharing company, told the story in 1988. A compiler at Tymshare was allowed to write files in its own directory, SYSX, so that it could update a statistics file. Users could also name a file to receive debugging output. One user named `(SYSX)BILL`, the billing file. The compiler opened it with its own authority and overwrote it. The billing information was lost.

Hardy's diagnosis: the compiler "runs with authority stemming from two sources", the user who invoked it and its own licence to write in SYSX, and "has no way to keep them apart". It is a **deputy** acting for someone else, and it got **confused** about whose authority applied to which request.

Hardy's proposed cure was **capabilities** in the older, object sense: an unforgeable reference that both names an object and carries the right to use it. If the user passes a handle to the output file instead of a name, the compiler can only write where the user could. (This is a different idea from Linux capabilities, which are slices of root.) The everyday version of the cure: when acting on a name chosen by the caller, act with the caller's authority, or have the caller pass an already-open file descriptor.

**PwnKit read as a confused deputy.** In linux-for-security you saw how `pkexec` (CVE-2021-4034), a setuid-root program, read and wrote one slot past the end of `argv` when called with no arguments, and so re-inserted an environment variable the dynamic linker had just removed. Look at it through Hardy's lens: pkexec held root's authority to do privileged work for polkit, but it also carried the caller's arguments and environment. A bug let the caller's input steer root's authority. Every setuid program is a deputy in this sense, which is why sudo (lesson 7) and pkexec make such valuable targets, and why `no_new_privs` (setuid stops working) is such a strong control for services.

**TOCTOU** (time of check to time of use) is a race: a program checks a condition, then acts on it, and the world changes in between. The `access(2)` manual page warns that using `access()` to check whether the user may open a file before calling `open()` "creates a security hole", because the user can change the file in the gap.

The classic shape is a setuid-root program that checks with the *real* UID (`access`) and then opens with the *effective* UID (root). If an attacker swaps the path for a symbolic link to `/etc/passwd` between the two calls, root opens the wrong file.

blocks.title: A check-then-use race on one path (not to scale)

scenes.caption: Honest case: a setuid logger checks that the user may write the path, then opens it as root and appends. Path and file stay the same throughout.
Attack: in the gap between check and use, the user replaces the path with a symlink to /etc/passwd. The check passed on the old file; root opens the new one.
Fix: no separate check. The program opens the file with the caller's own identity and O_NOFOLLOW, so the kernel's check and the use are one atomic step. The swap gains nothing.

blocks.caption: The fix is the one access(2) itself recommends: temporarily switch the effective UID to the real UID and then call open. Both versions compile on macOS (checked). O_NOFOLLOW refuses a symbolic link as the last path component.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.** The kernel helps too: with `fs.protected_symlinks = 1` a symlink in a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp` is followed only if its owner matches the follower or the directory owner. The kernel docs describe these link races as "a long-standing class of security issues". `fs.protected_hardlinks` and `fs.protected_regular` close related tricks. seccomp filters are immune to this class by design: BPF programs cannot dereference pointers, so there is no second read that could see different data.

For review, look for these smells: `access()` or `stat()` followed by `open()` on the same path, privileged code that acts on caller-supplied names, and files created in shared directories with predictable names.

blocks.question: A root-owned backup daemon accepts a destination path from any local user and writes the backup there with its own root authority. What is the core flaw?
options: It runs too often
It is a confused deputy: it applies its own authority to an object the caller chose, so callers can make it overwrite files they could not write
The backup is not encrypted
It should use TCP instead
blocks.explain: Hardy's compiler again. The fix is to open the destination with the caller's authority, or to have the caller hand over an open descriptor, so the daemon cannot be steered to files the caller has no right to.

blocks.question: Which change removes the TOCTOU window in a setuid program that calls access() then open()?
options: Dropping the separate check and opening the file with the caller's own effective UID (and O_NOFOLLOW)
Adding sleep() between the calls
Calling access() twice
Checking that the path string does not contain /etc
blocks.explain: Any separate check leaves a gap. Making the open itself run with the caller's identity lets the kernel do the check atomically on the file actually opened.

lessons.title: Kernel bugs and container escapes: Dirty Pipe and runc

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 claimed kernel bugs are the worst bugs. Here are two real cases, one in the kernel and one in the container runtime, and what each layer of this course did or did not do about them.

**Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847).** Max Kellermann, a developer at the hosting company CM4all (part of IONOS), started from a support ticket in April 2021 about corrupt log files. By February 2022 Kellermann had traced it to a Linux kernel bug that lets an unprivileged process **overwrite data in arbitrary read-only files**. Kellermann's summary: it is similar to Dirty COW but easier to exploit.

Three kernel ideas make it understandable:

- The **page cache** is the kernel's in-memory copy of file contents. Reads are served from it; writes change it and are later written back to disk.
- A **pipe** is a kernel buffer between two processes, organised as a ring of `pipe_buffer` entries, each pointing to a page.
- `splice()` moves data from a file into a pipe without copying: the pipe buffer simply points at the file's page in the page cache.

Pipe buffers holding ordinary written data carry a flag, `PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE`, that lets the next small write be appended into the same page. A page borrowed from the page cache must never have that flag. Kernel 4.9 (2016) added code that created pipe buffers without initialising their flags, harmless at the time. Kernel 5.8 (2020) turned merge permission into that per-buffer flag, and the stale value became dangerous.

blocks.title: Dirty Pipe: a stale flag on a borrowed page (simplified)

scenes.caption: A pipe is a ring of buffers inside the kernel. Each buffer has a flags field. CAN_MERGE means a later write may be appended into this buffer's page.
Ordinary data written into a pipe sits in anonymous pages that belong to the pipe, so merging writes into them is correct.
When the data is read out, the buffers are freed, but the flags field is left as it was. Nothing is wrong yet.
splice() puts a reference to a cached page of a read-only file into a slot. The code that set up this buffer never initialised flags, so the stale CAN_MERGE survives.
A later write() to the pipe sees CAN_MERGE and copies into that page: the kernel's in-memory copy of a read-only file. Pipe writes never check file permissions.
The fix sets flags = 0 whenever such a buffer is created. The file page is never mergeable, so a write goes into a new anonymous buffer instead.

blocks.md:
Kellermann notes it works without write permission, on immutable files, on read-only btrfs snapshots and on read-only mounts, "because the page cache is always writable (by the kernel), and writing to a pipe never checks any permissions". Permission bits, setuid hygiene and read-only mounts are all checks the kernel does on the normal path, and this path skipped them. Overwriting the cached copy of a setuid-root program or a root-owned configuration file is enough for root.

A quieter detail matters for responders: overwriting the page cache this way does not mark the page dirty, so the change may never reach the disk. It can vanish after a reboot or when memory is reclaimed, leaving little for disk forensics.

blocks.caption: The whole fix: two lines that initialise a field. Bugs of the class 'uninitialised memory' can sleep for years until another change gives the stale value a meaning.

blocks.md:
Timeline from the disclosure: the bug report, patch and proof went to the kernel security team on 20 February 2022; fixed stable kernels 5.16.11, 5.15.25 and 5.10.102 followed on 23 February; it was reproduced on a Google Pixel 6 and reported to Android's security team on 21 February; public disclosure was 7 March 2022. Affected: Linux 5.8 and later until those fixes.

**Defender view.** Patch the kernel and reboot (a running kernel is not fixed by installing a package). No LSM policy, capability drop or user namespace stops a kernel bug reachable from an allowed system call; only a separate kernel (lesson 13) changes the picture. Because the write may never hit the disk, file-integrity scanners can miss it.

**runc CVE-2019-5736.** On 11 February 2019 Aleksa Sarai of SUSE, a runc maintainer, announced a breakout found by Adam Iwaniuk and Borys Popławski. A malicious container could **overwrite the host's runc binary** and so gain root on the host the next time runc ran. It needed only the ability to run any command as root inside a container, either by starting a container from an attacker-controlled image or when an admin ran `docker exec` into a container the attacker had written to. NVD's description: "file-descriptor mishandling, related to /proc/self/exe". Affected runc through 1.0-rc6, as used in Docker before 18.09.2.

The idea at concept level: while runc enters a container to start a process, that process is briefly the host's runc program running inside the container's namespaces, and its `/proc/<pid>/exe` link points at the host's runc file. Container code that can reach that handle can write to the host binary. The Leaky Vessels advisory names the same `/proc/<pid>/exe` route as the path to overwriting host binaries.

blocks.title: runc CVE-2019-5736: a host binary visible from inside

scenes.caption: An administrator runs docker exec. The host's runc binary starts and begins entering the container's namespaces.
Inside the container, runc's /proc entry is visible, and its exe link refers to the host file /usr/bin/runc, not to anything in the image.
Root in the container uses that handle to rewrite the host binary. The next runc invocation on the host runs the attacker's code as host root.
Fix (runc commit 0a8e4117): runc first copies itself into a sealed memfd (an in-memory file that can be locked against writes) and runs from that, so /proc/self/exe points at a throwaway copy.
Layers that also stopped it, per the advisory: user namespaces with host root unmapped, and SELinux when containers ran as container_t. Not stopped by default AppArmor.

blocks.md: **Defender view for both.** Inventory and patch the kernel and the container runtime: they are the boundary. Run containers rootless or with user namespaces so container root is not host root. Keep SELinux or AppArmor on and check which domain containers actually run in. Use only trusted images and be careful with `docker exec` into containers that ran untrusted code. For hostile multi-tenant code, move the boundary to gVisor or a microVM. For both bugs the reliable detection signal is the installed version, not a log line.

blocks.question: Why did permission bits and a read-only mount fail to stop Dirty Pipe?
options: Read-only mounts only apply to root
They were misconfigured on the affected hosts
Those checks run on the normal file write path; Dirty Pipe changed the page cache through a pipe write, which never checks file permissions
Dirty Pipe disabled SELinux first
blocks.explain: The kernel enforces permissions where it expects writes to happen. A kernel bug that reaches the data by another path bypasses every check, which is the reason kernel bugs rank highest.

blocks.question: Which setting, according to the runc maintainers, blocked CVE-2019-5736?
options: Docker's default seccomp profile
The default AppArmor profile
A read-only container root filesystem
Running containers in user namespaces where host root is not mapped into the container
blocks.explain: The advisory says the attack is not blocked by default AppArmor (nor by Fedora's moby-engine SELinux domain), but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then an unprivileged host UID that cannot write /usr/bin/runc.

lessons.title: Putting it together: one service, many layers

blocks.md: No single mechanism in this course is enough, and each has failed somewhere. The working answer is layers, each assuming the one in front of it has already fallen. systemd, the Linux service manager from linux-for-security, can apply most of these layers to any service with a few lines in its unit file ([systemd.exec(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html)).

blocks.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/webd.service   (Linux only)
# systemd allows comments only on their own lines, never after a value
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/webd
# lesson 7: not root
User=webd
# lesson 6: the one power it needs, and nothing else, ever
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
# lesson 7: setuid and file capabilities stop working
NoNewPrivileges=yes
# lessons 10-11: filesystem read-only, homes hidden, own /tmp
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/webd
# lesson 14: no module loading, /proc/sys and friends read-only
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
# lesson 10: no new namespaces

blocks.caption: Directive meanings from systemd.exec(5). @system-service is documented as the recommended starting point for allow-listing system calls for system services. Add an SELinux domain or AppArmor profile on top for MAC.

blocks.md: Read the unit as a list of answers to "what if the parser is exploited?". The attacker runs as an unprivileged user with one capability that cannot grow (`NoNewPrivileges`, bounding set); setuid helpers such as pkexec or sudo will not raise them, so PwnKit and Baron Samedit gain nothing from inside this service. The filesystem is read-only apart from one directory, so persistence is hard. Many dangerous syscalls fail with EPERM. What remains is the kernel itself, through the syscalls still allowed, plus whatever the service's own data is worth.

blocks.title: Which control stops or contains each case (documented or inferred)

scenes.caption: 1 means the control stops or contains the case: documented by a course source, except the no_new_privs and microVM cells, which are inferred from how those controls work. 0 means no source here says so. Only patching fixes every one.
no_new_privs neutralises the setuid route used by PwnKit and Baron Samedit, but a kernel bug like Dirty Pipe ignores it.
Inferred: a separate kernel contains a host-kernel-class bug. In a microVM the bug compromises the guest kernel, not the host (gVisor, lesson 13, also keeps apps off the host kernel).
For runc CVE-2019-5736 the advisory names user namespaces and SELinux's container_t domain. Leaky Vessels' workarounds (cwd /, trusted images) are not in these columns.

blocks.md:
**Where to practise (legally).** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Good free places to try these mechanisms hands-on:

- [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/) has free structured modules that include sandboxing and kernel security, run in its own lab environment.
- [OverTheWire](https://overthewire.org/wargames/) (start with Bandit) drills Linux permissions, setuid programs and the shell on servers built for the purpose.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF, Carnegie Mellon University) is a beginner capture-the-flag with general skills and binary challenges.

On your own Linux VM: write a small server, then add the unit directives above one at a time and watch what breaks; read `grep Cap /proc/<pid>/status` and `Seccomp:` before and after; put one profile in AppArmor complain mode and read the log it produces.

Assume each layer will fail and ask what the next one still guarantees: least privilege inside the program (privsep, drops), MAC around it, seccomp and capabilities on its kernel access, namespaces and cgroups around its view, and a separate kernel when the code is hostile. Patching is the layer under all of them.

blocks.question: A service unit has NoNewPrivileges=yes and runs as an unprivileged user. An attacker in the service runs the vulnerable pkexec from PwnKit. What happens?
options: They get root, because pkexec is setuid
pkexec runs without its setuid privilege, so the bug yields nothing beyond the service user's rights
systemd restarts the service
pkexec refuses to start
blocks.explain: With no_new_privs set, execve does not honour setuid bits or file capabilities, so pkexec runs as the service user. The memory bug still exists but gains nothing; the same holds for sudo and Baron Samedit.

blocks.question: You must run customer-supplied code on shared hosts. Which choice best matches the threat?
options: chroot jails
Plain containers with the default profiles
Containers with --privileged for compatibility
gVisor or Firecracker microVMs, with patched runtimes and kernels, because a host kernel bug should not be directly reachable
blocks.explain: Hostile multi-tenant code calls for a boundary that does not rely on the full host kernel. Plain containers share it, --privileged removes most protections, and chroot is not a security boundary.
